title: ARM vs x86 Architecture
summary: ARM utilizes a power-efficient Reduced Instruction Set (RISC), whereas x86 uses a Complex Instruction Set (CISC) optimized for peak raw throughput.

body.definition: The abstract model of a computer that defines the supported data types, registers, memory architecture, and machine instructions executable by the processor.

body.text: The x86 architecture, developed by Intel and AMD, is CISC-based with variable-length instructions and dedicated hardware decoders. ARM is a RISC architecture that uses fixed-length, single-cycle instructions, minimizing silicon die size and thermal power dissipation for mobile and high-density server platforms.
Architectural Differences

rows.label: Memory Access
values: Instructions can directly access memory operands

body.text: Modern high-end x86 cores internally decode complex CISC instructions into simpler RISC-like micro-operations (uops) before dispatching to execution units.

title: 32-Bit vs 64-Bit Computing
summary: 64-bit processors use wider registers and memory addresses, breaking the 4 GB RAM limit of 32-bit systems to address over 18 quintillion bytes.

body.definition: The natural data width and register size that a CPU processor core can manipulate in a single native arithmetic operation.

body.text: A 32-bit register can reference 2^32 distinct memory addresses, creating a theoretical ceiling of 4,294,967,296 bytes (4 GB) of addressable physical RAM. A 64-bit processor (x86-64 / AArch64) expands addressable space to 2^64 bytes (16 Exabytes), enabling massive in-memory databases and virtualization.
Key Advantages of 64-Bit Architecture

items: Dramatically expanded integer math precision without multi-instruction emulation.
Doubled general-purpose register count (e.g., 8 to 16 in x86-64, 31 in ARM64) reducing stack memory spills.
Hardware-enforced security features such as Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) entropy.

body.text: 64-bit pointers occupy 8 bytes of memory compared to 4 bytes on 32-bit systems, slightly increasing memory consumption for pointer-heavy data structures.

title: CPU Clock Speed & IPC
summary: Clock speed measures how many electrical cycles a processor completes per second, while IPC determines how many instructions execute per cycle.

body.definition: The rate at which a crystal oscillator pulses the synchronous clock signal coordinating transistor transitions across a microprocessor.

body.text: A processor operating at 4.0 GHz pulses four billion clock cycles every second. However, clock speed alone does not determine real-world speed: performance is the product of Clock Speed multiplied by Instructions Per Cycle (IPC). An older 5.0 GHz CPU can be outpaced by a newer 3.5 GHz CPU with higher IPC.
Base vs Boost Clock

items: Base Clock: Guaranteed sustainable operating frequency under continuous heavy multi-threaded workloads within thermal design limits (TDP).
Boost/Turbo Clock: Opportunistic high frequency reached on single or bursty cores when thermal and electrical power headroom allows.

body.text: Dynamic Frequency Scaling (DVFS) adjusts clock speed and core voltage hundreds of times per second based on workload demand to conserve energy.

title: CPU Cache Hierarchy (L1, L2, L3)
summary: CPU cache is ultra-fast static SRAM placed directly on the processor die to prevent execution cores from idling while waiting for slow main memory.

body.definition: High-speed volatile on-die memory built from 6-transistor flip-flop cells that retains data without needing periodic refresh cycles.

body.text: Fetching instructions from system RAM takes roughly 50 to 100 nanoseconds (~200 CPU cycles). To bridge this latency gap, processors maintain a multi-tier cache hierarchy holding recently referenced code and memory blocks according to spatial and temporal locality principles.
Cache Tiers Compared

rows.label: L3 Cache
values: Shared across all cores on die

body.text: A cache miss forces the CPU memory controller to request data from the next cache tier or main DRAM, stalling pipeline execution.

title: Thermal Throttling & TJMax
summary: Thermal throttling is a hardware-level safety mechanism that automatically reduces processor clock speeds and voltages when operating temperatures exceed safe limits.

body.definition: The maximum silicon junction temperature specified by silicon manufacturers before internal protective thermal throttling or emergency shutdown engages.

body.text: When silicon transistors conduct electrical current, resistance generates thermal dissipation. If the cooling subsystem (heatsink, fan, vapor chamber) cannot evacuate heat as fast as it is generated, on-die thermal sensors trigger throttling to prevent permanent chip degradation.
Throttling Stages

items: Dynamic Downclocking: The CPU governor drops clock multiplier and voltage to reduce thermal output (P = C * V^2 * f).
Duty Cycle Skipping: Core clock pulses are deliberately dropped to decrease active execution time.
PROCHOT Trip & Hard Cutoff: If temperatures continue rising toward 105C - 115C, the power delivery circuit immediately cuts voltage to prevent catastrophic damage.

body.text: Mobile devices and slim laptops rely heavily on burst performance, intentionally throttling down by 20-40% during sustained gaming or rendering sessions.

title: Semiconductor Process Nodes (nm)
summary: Process nodes measure silicon fabrication density and lithography milestones, allowing billions of smaller transistors to operate with higher efficiency.

body.definition: A specific generation of semiconductor manufacturing process characterized by transistor density, gate architecture (e.g. FinFET, GAAFET), and lithography resolution.

body.text: Historically, node names like '7nm' or '3nm' measured gate lengths. Today, node names are marketing designations for generational density improvements achieved using Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography and multi-patterning on silicon wafers.
Transistor Architectures

items: Planar FET: Classic flat 2D transistor used down to the 28nm node before quantum tunneling leakage became unmanageable.
FinFET: 3D fin-shaped channel wrapped by the gate on three sides, dominating 22nm down to 3nm nodes.
GAAFET / Nanosheet: Gate-All-Around nanosheets wrapped on all four sides for maximum electrostatic control at 2nm and beyond.

body.text: Shrinking transistor dimensions lowers switching capacitance, enabling higher clock frequencies at reduced core operating voltages.

title: Multi-Core Processors & Heterogeneous Cores
summary: Multi-core processors combine multiple independent execution cores on a single chip, utilizing symmetric or heterogeneous big.LITTLE topologies.

body.definition: A single integrated circuit containing two or more independent execution micro-cores capable of running separate program threads concurrently.

body.text: When single-core clock scaling hit thermal limits (the 'Power Wall') in the mid-2000s, chip designers pivoted to parallelism. Multiple cores allow operating systems to distribute concurrent threads across cores simultaneously without driving clocks to extreme thermal thresholds.
Heterogeneous Core Topology (big.LITTLE)

items: Performance Cores (P-Cores): Out-of-order, wide-decode pipelines designed for maximum single-thread responsiveness and heavy math.
Efficiency Cores (E-Cores): In-order or compact micro-architectures dedicated to background OS services, audio streaming, and light tasks at minimal power.

body.text: Amdahl's Law dictates that the speedup from multi-core parallelism is strictly constrained by the sequential, non-parallelizable portions of software algorithms.
